lessons.title: Racing the beam: the Atari 2600 draws one line at a time
lessons.summary: How Atari 2600 games drew with no frame buffer by rewriting the graphics chip between scanlines, within 76 CPU cycles per line.

lessons.title: Space Invaders: the march that speeds up as you shoot
lessons.summary: Why Space Invaders speeds up as you shoot: it redraws one invader per screen refresh, so fewer invaders means faster marching.

lessons.title: Asteroids: drawing with a vector beam
lessons.summary: How Asteroids drew with no pixels: a chip traces a list of beam moves about 60 times a second, so cost follows lines, not dots.

lessons.title: Pac-Man's level 256: one byte too small
lessons.summary: Why Pac-Man's level 256 is a garbled half maze: a one-byte level count wraps to zero and the fruit loop writes 256 times over the screen.

lessons.title: Donkey Kong's level 22: a timer that wraps to almost nothing
lessons.summary: Why Donkey Kong ends at level 22: the bonus timer is worked out in one byte, 260 wraps to 4, and the cap that should catch it checks too late.

lessons.title: ZX Spectrum attribute clash: two colours per 8 by 8 block
lessons.summary: Why ZX Spectrum sprites stain the scenery: colour is stored once per 8 by 8 block, so a moving sprite repaints every block it touches.

lessons.title: NES sprite flicker: eight sprites per line, shared out by turns
lessons.summary: Why NES sprites flicker: the chip draws only the first 8 sprites on each line, so games reshuffle the list every frame and let everyone take turns.

lessons.title: Super Mario Bros.: the cloud and the bush share their tiles
lessons.summary: Why Super Mario Bros. bushes look like clouds: NES tiles store colour numbers, not colours, so one shape drawn with two palettes became two objects.

lessons.title: Pokémon Red and Blue: MissingNo. and one block of memory with two jobs
lessons.summary: Why MissingNo. appears: the old man's tutorial parks your name in the wild Pokémon table, and one stretch of shore reads that leftover list.

lessons.title: Amiga copper gradients: a new colour on every line
lessons.summary: How Amiga skies got dozens of shades from a tiny palette: a coprocessor rewrites one colour register as the screen is drawn, line by line.

lessons.title: Out Run: a 3D road drawn one line at a time
lessons.summary: How Out Run's road looks 3D with no polygons: each screen line is one flat strip at one depth, shifted and sized from a table built every frame.

lessons.title: Prince of Persia: a run cycle traced from film
lessons.summary: How Prince of Persia got lifelike running: poses traced from video of a real runner, each with its own step, then reused for the shadow double.

lessons.title: F-Zero and Mode 7: a flat map tilted into a racetrack
lessons.summary: How the Super Nintendo's Mode 7 turns one flat track map into a floor in perspective by giving every screen line its own scale.

lessons.title: Sonic the Hedgehog: many layers of parallax from one background
lessons.summary: How Sonic's backgrounds slide at many speeds on a chip with two layers: a table gives every screen line of one background its own scroll value.

lessons.title: Sonic the Hedgehog: running round a loop with two sensors and one speed
lessons.summary: How Sonic runs up walls and round loops: one speed along the ground, two sensors that read its angle, and a rule that drops him below 2.5 px per frame.

lessons.title: Another World: a whole game drawn from lists of points
lessons.summary: How Another World fit cinematic animation on two floppy disks: shapes stored as a few points and filled row by row at play time, not as pixels.
